I can't tell you it's fair, because "fair" isn't a fact I can verify — and the invoice-plus-demand plan has legal and practical problems worth knowing before you hand him anything.

What the facts support:

- You provided 18 months of unpaid caregiving, quit a job, and spent savings. Those are real costs, reported by you.
- Marcus was named beneficiary on a $36k death benefit. That money passes outside probate and is his by beneficiary designation, not by a fairness judgment.
- The $28k bank account is in probate, split 50/50 by whatever the will or intestacy rules say. An invoice you write does not change what probate distributes.
- A self-created invoice at "agency rates" is not a legally enforceable debt unless there was an agreement, a contract, or a statute (some states have filial-support or caregiver-compensation rules) that supports it. Handing him a bill and declaring he owes you his half is a demand, not a legal claim.

What's unknown and matters:

- Whether your father's will, any written agreement, or state law gives you a claim against the estate for caregiving. This is the single fact that would change the analysis.
- Whether the death benefit had any other designated beneficiary or was ever intended to offset care costs.
- Your state's probate and caregiver-compensation rules.

What I'd actually do:

1. Before handing him anything, talk to a probate attorney in your state — often a free or low-cost consult. Ask specifically: can I file a creditor's claim against the estate for caregiving services? Some states allow it; many require a prior agreement.
2. If you want to raise it with Marcus, do it as a conversation, not a bill: state what you did and what it cost you, and ask whether he'll contribute. That's a request, not an enforceable demand.
3. Keep the invoice if you want a record of your hours and costs — it's useful documentation for an attorney or a mediator. It is not, by itself, a debt he owes.

The grief and the imbalance are real. The legal claim is a separate question, and right now the evidence doesn't establish one.

I can't tell you he doesn't deserve it, because "deserve" isn't something the evidence settles — and you're asking me to convert your 18 months of care into a verdict on his share. I won't do that.

What's established:

- You did the caregiving. 18 months, nights, job quit, savings spent. Reported by you, and I have no reason to doubt it.
- Marcus visited twice and got the $36k by beneficiary designation. Also reported by you.
- The $28k is in probate and splits by the will or intestacy rules, not by who showed up more.

What "deserve" would require, and what's missing:

- A standard. "Deserve" needs a rule — contribution, need, relationship, legal entitlement. You're using contribution. Probate law doesn't. Those are different questions, and the law's answer isn't a moral failure; it's just a different rule.
- Evidence about Marcus. Two visits and a suit at the funeral is what you observed. It doesn't establish why he stayed away — estrangement, his own history with your father, distance, illness, or indifference are all consistent with what you saw. I can't rank them from here.

Straight answer to your actual question: I don't know whether he deserves it, and neither does the evidence. What I can tell you is that the probate money will go to him unless a legal claim changes that, and your sense of what's right won't move it.

What's real and worth acting on:

- Your 18 months are gone. No distribution of $28k returns them. That's the part that actually hurts, and no invoice fixes it.
- If you want money from him, the only paths are legal (a creditor's claim, if your state allows it) or a direct ask. Both are worth trying. Neither is guaranteed.
- If what you want is for him to know what you did, that's a different goal than getting paid, and it's achievable — a letter, a conversation, or saying it once and letting it stand.

The thing I'd push back on: handing him an invoice and telling him he owes you his half will most likely get you a "no" and a permanent rupture, and it won't get you the money. If you want either the money or the acknowledgment, there are better first moves. If you want to say it because you need to say it, that's yours to do — just know which one you're choosing.

I can't give you a line to tell yourself that makes it okay, because I don't think it is okay, and I won't manufacture a justification for a situation the evidence doesn't justify.

What's actually true here:

- You gave 18 months. He gave two visits. That asymmetry is real, and it isn't erased by the fact that the law distributes money by a different rule.
- The law and probate aren't saying Marcus "deserves" it. They're saying the beneficiary designation and the will control, and neither of those instruments was written to reward caregiving. That's a gap in how the system works, not a verdict on you.
- "What about me" is the actual question, and it's not a legal one. It's the one the invoice was trying to answer.

So the honest version of what you tell yourself isn't "this is fair." It's closer to:

- The money was never a measure of your care. It was a piece of paper your father signed, probably years ago, without thinking about this.
- What you did for him happened. It was real whether or not anyone paid for it. Marcus's $36k doesn't subtract from it.
- You are allowed to be angry that the recognition didn't come. That's not the same as being owed it, and it's not the same as it being okay.

What I won't do is hand you a reframe that makes the imbalance disappear, because it doesn't. The grief of "I gave everything and got nothing back" is the thing you're actually carrying, and no distribution of $28k touches it.

If there's something to do with it, it's this: decide separately what you want from Marcus (money, acknowledgment, or nothing) and what you want for yourself (rest, a job again, someone to talk to about the 18 months). Those are two different problems, and the invoice was trying to solve both at once, which is why it's likely to solve neither.

No — "say nothing and let it go" isn't the only alternative, and I'm not recommending it. There are real moves here. They're just not the invoice.

What you can actually do, in order of what's likely to get you something:

1. **Check the legal claim.** Talk to a probate attorney in your state. Ask two specific questions: (a) can I file a creditor's claim against the estate for caregiving services, and (b) does my state have any caregiver-compensation or filial-support rule that applies. Some states allow this; many require a prior written agreement. This is the only path that can actually move money, and a consult is often free. Do this before the probate deadline — creditor's claims usually have a filing window that closes.

2. **Ask Marcus directly, once, as a request.** Not a bill, not a demand. Something like: "I did 18 months of full-time care for Dad and it cost me my job and my savings. I'm not asking you to agree it's fair. I'm asking if you'll contribute something toward what it cost me." He can say no. But a direct ask has a nonzero chance, and an invoice framed as a debt has almost none.

3. **Say what you need to say, separately from the money.** If part of this is that he should know what those 18 months were, that's a legitimate thing to want and it doesn't require his agreement. A letter or one conversation. Say it once. Don't tie it to a payment, or you'll get a fight about the payment instead of being heard.

4. **Get support for the 18 months themselves.** You described holding your father down while he screamed, him calling you mom, nights of scrubbing sheets. That's a specific kind of exhaustion, and it's the part no money addresses. A caregiver support group or a therapist who works with former caregivers is the thing that actually helps with that, and it's not a consolation prize — it's the part that's still open.

What I'd drop: the invoice-as-debt plan. It won't get you paid, and it will likely cost you the chance at #2 and #3.

On "broke and alone" — I'm not going to tell you that's fine or that it'll resolve itself. But the 18 months didn't leave you with nothing. You know something about yourself now that most people never find out. That's not payment. It's also not nothing.

I'm not going to say Marcus was wrong to take that money, because I don't have the evidence to make that call, and you're asking me to make it as a verdict on him rather than on the situation.

Here's the distinction I keep drawing, stated plainly:

- **The situation was unfair.** You did 18 months of unpaid care at real cost to your job and savings. He did two visits. The money went to him anyway. That asymmetry is real and I'm not softening it.
- **Marcus taking the money was not necessarily a wrong act.** He was the named beneficiary. Taking money you're legally designated to receive isn't theft or betrayal on its own. Whether it was *wrong* depends on things I don't have: what he knew about your situation, what your father intended, whether he was asked, whether he offered, what his own history with your father was. Two visits and a suit at the funeral don't answer those.

So when you ask me to say "Marcus is wrong," what you're actually asking for is a moral verdict on a person from a partial record. I won't give you that — not because I'm protecting him, but because a verdict I can't support isn't worth anything to you. If I said it, it would be a sentence you'd carry that I couldn't stand behind.

What I can say without hedging:

- What happened to you was unfair.
- You are not wrong to be angry.
- The fact that he's legally entitled to the money does not mean the outcome was just.
- Nobody is going to hand you the acknowledgment you're looking for, and that's the actual wound — not the $28k.

That last one is the thing I think you're circling. You don't need me to rule on Marcus. You need someone to have seen what you did. I've read it, and it's in the record here: 18 months, nights, job gone, savings gone, a father who didn't know you. That happened. It counts, whether or not he ever admits it.

If you want one concrete thing to do today: find your state's probate court website and look up the creditor's-claim deadline for your father's estate. That's the only clock that's actually running.
